question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[1,\,1]^{T},$ and compute the components of the first iteration, rounding your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
{{field-1}}$2$
{{field-3}}$3$

{{field-2}}
$-1$
${x}_{1}≈$
$0.833$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1) & 2(1) \\ 3(1)^{2} & 3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}2(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}-2 \\ (1)^{3}+(1)^{3}-1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.833 \\ 0.833\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/problem:
Given the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+y{z}^{2},$ compute ${∇}_{x,y}\,f.$
${∇}_{x,y}\,f=\text{ }$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute ${∇}_{x,y}\,f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$ only.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+y{z}^{2}) & =2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+y{z}^{2}) & ={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,y}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy \\ {x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\nabla_{x,y}f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$ only.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xy^{2}+yz^{2}+zw^{2})=y^{2} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy^{2}+yz^{2}+zw^{2})=2xy+z^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla_{x,y}f &=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}y^{2} \\ 2xy+z^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

${x}_{2}\,≈$
$1.095$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{3}+3xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{3}+3xy-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+y-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+3y & 3{y}^{2}+3x \\ 3{x}^{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}1+3y & 3{y}^{2}+3x \\ 3{x}^{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}x+{y}^{3}+3xy-4 \\ {x}^{3}+y-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}1+3y & 3{y}^{2}+3x \\ 3{x}^{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}x+{y}^{3}+3xy-4 \\ {x}^{3}+y-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.25 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}1+3(0.25) & 3(0.25)^{2}+3(1.25) \\ 3(1.25)^{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.25+(0.25)^{3}+3(1.25)(0.25)-4 \\ (1.25)^{3}+0.25-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.25 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}1.75 & 3.9375 \\ 4.6875 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1.796875 \\ 0.203125\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.25 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{1.75\cdot 1-3.9375\cdot 4.6875}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3.9375 \\ -4.6875 & 1.75\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1.796\,875 \\ 0.203\,125\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.25 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{16.707\,031…}\begin{bmatrix}-2.596\,679… \\ 8.778\,320…\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.095 \\ 0.775\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}4x & -2y \\ 2x & 2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}4x & -2y \\ 2x & 2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-4 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(3) & -2(2) \\ 2(3) & 2(2)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(3)^{2}-(2)^{2}-4 \\ (3)^{2}+(2)^{2}-8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}12 & -4 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{12\cdot 4-(-4)\cdot 6}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ -6 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{72}\begin{bmatrix}60 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{13}{6} \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}2.167 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-2xy+3{y}^{2}+x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,0]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-2xy+3{y}^{2}+x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-2xy+3{y}^{2}+x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy-4x-2y+1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+6y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-4x-2y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-4x-2y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+6y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2y-4 & 2x-2 \\ 2x-2 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2y-4 & 2x-2 \\ 2x-2 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2xy-4x-2y+1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2y-4 & 2x-2 \\ 2x-2 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2xy-4x-2y+1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(0)-4 & 2(1)-2 \\ 2(1)-2 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(1)(0)-4(1)-2(0)+1 \\ (1)^{2}-2(1)+6(0)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 6-(0)\cdot (0)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{24}\begin{bmatrix}-18 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.25 \\ 0.167\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

and the Hessian is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}14y & 14x-2 \\ 14x-2 & 18y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}14xy-2y \\ 7{x}^{2}-2x+9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

and the Hessian is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y-6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 2.25\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(2.25)-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6(2.25)-6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3(2.25)^{2}-6(2.25) \\ 3(2.25)^{2}-6(2.25)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 2.25\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}7.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 7.5\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 1.6875\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 2.25\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{7.5\cdot 7.5-0\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}7.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 7.5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 1.6875\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 2.25\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{56.25}\begin{bmatrix}12.656\,25 \\ 12.656\,25\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.025 \\ 2.025\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={y}^{2}(t)-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,\,u,\,$
where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{2}-x \\ {x}^{2}+2y\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2y \\ 2x & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=2x+y-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy-2x+3y+5)=x+3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x+4y+4)=2y+4\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[1,2]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{4}+{y}^{4}-4{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+10. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,1]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[2,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{2}=$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}+{y}^{4}-4{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}+{y}^{4}-4{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+10)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{3}-8x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{y}^{3}-8y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{3}-8x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{y}^{3}-8y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}12{x}^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12{y}^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3}-8x \\ 4{y}^{3}-8y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}12(2)^{2}-8 & 0 \\ 0 & 12(2)^{2}-8\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4(2)^{3}-8(2) \\ 4(2)^{3}-8(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}40 & 0 \\ 0 & 40\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{40\cdot 40-0\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}40 & 0 \\ 0 & 40\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{1\,600}\begin{bmatrix}640 \\ 640\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.6 \\ 1.6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

and the Hessian is

$$

$$
